abstract: |
  Volatility is one of the most forecastable quantities in finance and the basis of risk budgeting, option pricing and the volatility-managed portfolios of Moreira and Muir (2017), which scale equity exposure down when volatility is high. I compare nineteen forecasts of next month's realised volatility of the US stock market: GARCH, RiskMetrics and the standard HAR regression as benchmarks; small regressions that add the VIX and credit conditions; and ridge, lasso, partial least squares, random forests, boosting and neural networks on about 140 real-time predictors. Forecasts are made at every month-end from January 2000 to July 2026 using only data available at the time. The month-end VIX is the best single predictor: it explains 52% of the variation in next month's log realised variance against 43% for HAR, and the machine-learning models do no better than the VIX plus credit spreads. The advantage appears only after 2013; in 2000–2012 the VIX was no better than HAR. On QLIKE, the loss best suited to variance, a GJR-GARCH model with Student-t errors scores best, and nearly all models stay in the 10% Model Confidence Set, so the data cannot separate them. Accuracy does not carry over to money. Managing exposure by any of ten forecasters shrinks the worst month (from −17% to between −12% and −15%) and the deepest drawdown but raises the Sharpe ratio from 0.49 only to 0.52–0.59, never with statistical significance, and the VIX-only forecast, among the most accurate, gives the weakest strategy.

```{python}
alt.renderers.enable("svg")
alt.data_transformers.disable_max_rows()
BLUE, ORANGE, GREY, GREEN, RED = "#1f4e79", "#e07b00", "#8c8c8c", "#2e7d32", "#c62828"

fc_all = pd.read_csv("results/forecasts.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
fc = fc_all[fc_all["actual"].notna()].reset_index(drop=True)
acc = pd.read_csv("results/accuracy.csv").set_index("key")
per = pd.read_csv("results/accuracy_by_period.csv")
strat = pd.read_csv("results/strategy.csv", index_col=0)

imp = pd.read_csv("results/importance_top.csv")
H = json.load(open("results/headline.json"))
N = M.NAMES
ann = lambda h: 100 * np.sqrt(12 * h)  # noqa: E731


def table(df: pd.DataFrame, fmt: dict) -> Markdown:
    d = df.copy()
    for c, f in fmt.items():
        d[c] = d[c].map(lambda v, f=f: "–" if pd.isna(v) else f.format(v + 0.0).replace("-0.0", "0.0"))
    return Markdown(d.to_markdown(index=False, disable_numparse=True))
```

# The question

When markets are calm, equities earn their premium with little risk; when volatility spikes, losses cluster. Volatility is also unusually predictable: high-volatility months are followed by high-volatility months, which is why risk models, option prices and volatility-targeting funds all rest on a forecast of it. Moreira and Muir (2017) showed that an investor who holds less of the stock market when volatility is high, and more when it is low, earns higher risk-adjusted returns. Whether that holds up depends on two things this study tests separately: how well volatility can be forecast in real time, and whether a better forecast makes the strategy better.

# Design

The models, settings and the strategy rule below were fixed before any out-of-sample result was computed. All nineteen forecasters are reported, including those that fail.

**Target.** The log of next month's realised variance of the US stock market: the sum of squared daily returns of the CRSP value-weighted market over the next calendar month (Kenneth French's data library, July 1926 to August 2026). Logs make the target close to normal and the forecast errors well behaved.

**Predictors (about 140).**

* Realised-volatility history: last month, the last quarter and the last year of realised volatility (the three HAR terms of Corsi 2009), the last five trading days, the share of variance from down days, the last day's move, and the last month's and year's return.
* Implied volatility: the VIX on the last trading day of the month, from 1990, and the FRED-MD monthly-average VIX.
* Credit and funding conditions: the Baa minus Treasury spread, the Gilchrist–Zakrajšek excess bond premium and spread, the Chicago Fed financial-conditions indexes, the St. Louis Fed stress index, term spreads, bank lending standards and delinquencies.
* The 126 series of FRED-MD (McCracken and Ng 2016), made stationary with the published transformation codes.

**Real-time information.** Market prices are as of the forecast date. Macro data, the excess bond premium and the financial-conditions indexes are lagged one month for publication; quarterly bank data a full quarter. A predictor enters only once it has five years of history in the training window. Missing values are imputed, outliers winsorised and predictors standardised using the training window alone.

**Forecasting.** Forecasts are made at every month-end from January 2000 to July 2026 (319 forecasts of the following month, February 2000 to August 2026) with an expanding window. At forecast date $t$ a model learns only from months whose outcome is known, so the most recent training row is dated $t-1$. Linear models are re-estimated every month; penalties and the nonlinear models every January.

**Forecasters.**

| Group | Model | Specification |
|---|---|---|
| Benchmarks | Last month | Next month's variance equals last month's |
| | EWMA | RiskMetrics: exponentially weighted daily squared returns, decay 0.94 |
| | GJR-GARCH-t | Asymmetric GARCH(1,1) of Glosten, Jagannathan and Runkle (1993) with Student-t errors, estimated each January on all earlier daily data; multi-day forecast by iterating the model |
| | HAR | OLS on last month, last 3 months and last 12 months of realised volatility |
| | HAR from 1927 | The same, estimated on every month back to 1927 |
| Small regressions | HAR + realised measures | Adds the last five days, downside share, last day's move and returns |
| | VIX alone | Month-end VIX as a variance |
| | HAR + VIX | |
| | HAR + VIX + credit | Adds the Baa spread, excess bond premium, NFCI and term spread |
| High-dimensional | Ridge, lasso, elastic net | All predictors; penalties by 5-fold time-series cross-validation |
| | Principal components | Own history plus 5 factors of the remaining predictors |
| | Partial least squares | 3 components |
| | Random forest, gradient boosting | 500 trees, minimum leaf 5; boosting depth 3 with early stopping |
| | Neural network | Two hidden layers (32, 16), L2 penalty, early stopping, average of 5 seeds |
| Combinations | Mean, median | Of the eight high-dimensional models |

**Accuracy.** Two measures. The out-of-sample $R^2$ on log realised variance against the expanding historical mean (Campbell and Thompson 2008), and against HAR, the standard benchmark. And the QLIKE loss (Patton 2011) on the variance itself,

$$\text{QLIKE} = \frac{RV}{h} - \ln\frac{RV}{h} - 1,$$

where $h$ is the variance forecast, obtained from the log forecast as $h = \exp(\hat\mu + \hat s^2/2)$ with $\hat s^2$ the variance of the model's own past errors. QLIKE is the loss that keeps the ranking of forecasters stable when realised variance is noisy. Tests: Diebold–Mariano (1995) against HAR with the Harvey–Leybourne–Newbold (1997) correction, and the Model Confidence Set (Hansen, Lunde and Nason 2011).

**Strategy.** Each month hold $w_t = \min\left(2,\; \sigma^*_t / \hat\sigma_{t+1}\right)$ units of the stock market and the rest in Treasury bills, where $\hat\sigma_{t+1}$ is the forecast volatility and $\sigma^*_t$ the market's average volatility up to date $t$ (so nothing is known in advance). Leverage is capped at 2. Returns are net of 10 basis points per unit traded and a 0.5% a year borrowing spread on leverage. The comparison is with holding the market. Sharpe ratios are compared with the Jobson–Korkie test with Memmel's (2003) correction, alphas by regressing on the market with Newey–West errors.

# Results: forecast accuracy

## The scoreboard

```{python}
#| label: tbl-accuracy
#| tbl-cap: "Out-of-sample forecasts of next month's volatility, January 2000 – July 2026. R²_OS against the expanding mean on log realised variance; QLIKE (lower is better); p-values one-sided, Diebold–Mariano against HAR. Bold: p < 0.05. ✓: in the 10% Model Confidence Set (QLIKE)."
rows = []
for m in M.MODELS:
    a = acc.loc[m]
    p_ql, p_mse = a["p (DM vs HAR, QLIKE)"], a["p (DM vs HAR, MSE)"]
    f = lambda v, p: ("–" if pd.isna(v) else (f"**{v:.1f}**" if p < 0.05 else f"{v:.1f}")) if True else ""  # noqa: E731
    rows.append({
        "Model": N[m] + (" ✓" if a["MCS p (QLIKE)"] > 0.10 else ""),
        "R²_OS (%)": f"{a['R²_OS (%)']:.1f}",
        "vs HAR (%)": "–" if m == "har" else f(a["R²_OS vs HAR (%)"], p_mse),
        "QLIKE": f"{a['QLIKE']:.3f}",
        "QLIKE vs HAR (%)": "–" if m == "har" else f(a["QLIKE vs HAR (%)"], p_ql),
    })
Markdown(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_markdown(index=False, disable_numparse=True))
```

```{python}
#| include: false
A = acc
top_r2 = A["R²_OS (%)"].idxmax()
best_ql = A["QLIKE"].idxmin()
n_in = int((A["MCS p (QLIKE)"] > 0.10).sum())
n_in_mse = int((A["MCS p (squared error)"] > 0.10).sum())
nl = ["rf", "gbm", "nn"]
```

Four patterns stand out.

*The VIX is the best single predictor.* The month-end VIX alone explains `{python} f"{A.loc['vix', 'R²_OS (%)']:.1f}"`% of the variation in next month's log realised variance, against `{python} f"{A.loc['har', 'R²_OS (%)']:.1f}"`% for HAR, an improvement of `{python} f"{A.loc['vix', 'R²_OS vs HAR (%)']:.0f}"`% in squared error (Diebold–Mariano p = `{python} f"{A.loc['vix', 'p (DM vs HAR, MSE)']:.3f}"`). Adding HAR to it does nothing (`{python} f"{A.loc['har_vix', 'R²_OS (%)']:.1f}"`%), so recent realised volatility contains no information that the options market has not already priced. The most accurate model by squared error, HAR with the VIX and credit conditions, reaches `{python} f"{A.loc[top_r2, 'R²_OS (%)']:.1f}"`%.

*Machine learning matches the VIX; it does not beat it.* Ridge regression on all predictors reaches `{python} f"{A.loc['ridge', 'R²_OS (%)']:.1f}"`% and the average of the eight high-dimensional models `{python} f"{A.loc['mean_ml', 'R²_OS (%)']:.1f}"`%, both in the same range as the VIX with credit spreads. The importance pattern explains why (@fig-importance): the models lean on the same few predictors, the three HAR terms, the five-day volatility and the VIX. The flexible nonlinear models do worse than the linear ones (random forest `{python} f"{A.loc['rf', 'R²_OS (%)']:.1f}"`%, boosting `{python} f"{A.loc['gbm', 'R²_OS (%)']:.1f}"`%, neural network `{python} f"{A.loc['nn', 'R²_OS (%)']:.1f}"`%): with a few hundred monthly observations there is not enough data to learn nonlinearities that a log transformation has already removed.

*On QLIKE the old GARCH model wins.* `{python} N[best_ql]` has the lowest QLIKE (`{python} f"{A.loc[best_ql, 'QLIKE']:.3f}"`, `{python} f"{-A.loc[best_ql, 'QLIKE vs HAR (%)']:.0f}"`% below HAR) although it uses nothing but daily returns. A plausible reason is that it reacts to the size of the latest daily moves in a way monthly regressions cannot, which matters for a loss that punishes underestimating variance heavily.

*The data cannot separate most models.* `{python} f"{n_in}"` of the 19 forecasters stay in the 10% Model Confidence Set on QLIKE and `{python} f"{n_in_mse}"` on squared error. Only the last-month forecast is excluded on QLIKE; on squared error the two HAR versions, the principal-components regression and the neural network drop out as well. The appropriate conclusion is a ranking by groups, not a winner.

## Where the VIX helps

```{python}
#| label: tbl-periods
#| tbl-cap: "R²_OS (%) against the expanding mean, by sub-period"
pp = per.pivot(index="Model", columns="Period", values="R²_OS (%)")
pp = pp.loc[[N[m] for m in ["ewma", "garch", "har", "har_x", "vix", "har_cred", "ridge", "mean_ml"]]].reset_index()
table(pp, {c: "{:.1f}" for c in pp.columns[1:]})
```

The VIX's advantage is concentrated in the second half. In 2000–2012 the VIX alone scored `{python} f"{pp.set_index('Model').loc[N['vix'], '2000-2012']:.0f}"`% against `{python} f"{pp.set_index('Model').loc[N['har'], '2000-2012']:.0f}"`% for HAR, and the models using realised measures from daily data (GARCH, HAR with extra measures, ridge) were the best; from 2013 the VIX models reach `{python} f"{pp.set_index('Model').loc[N['vix'], '2013-2026']:.0f}"`%, nearly double HAR's `{python} f"{pp.set_index('Model').loc[N['har'], '2013-2026']:.0f}"`%. Two reasons are plausible but not tested here: the VIX models start from only ten years of history in 2000, and the relationship between implied and realised volatility may have changed with the growth of volatility trading. The practical lesson is that "the VIX predicts volatility" is a statement about the past decade more than about the full record.

# Results: does a better forecast make a better strategy?

```{python}
#| label: tbl-strategy
#| tbl-cap: "Volatility-managed market versus buy and hold, February 2000 – August 2026, excess returns over Treasury bills, net of costs. Leverage capped at 2. Alpha: annual, from a regression on the market (Newey–West t-statistic). p: one-sided Jobson–Korkie–Memmel test that the Sharpe ratio exceeds the market's."
s = strat.reset_index().rename(columns={"index": "Strategy"})
s["Strategy"] = s["Strategy"].replace({"Buy and hold": "Buy and hold the market"})
s["Alpha (t)"] = s.apply(lambda r: "–" if pd.isna(r["Alpha (% p.a.)"]) else f"{r['Alpha (% p.a.)']:.1f} ({r['Alpha t-stat']:.1f})", axis=1)
table(s[["Strategy", "Mean (% p.a.)", "Volatility (% p.a.)", "Sharpe ratio", "Worst month (%)", "Max drawdown (%)", "Average exposure", "Alpha (t)", "p (Sharpe > market)"]],
      {"Mean (% p.a.)": "{:.1f}", "Volatility (% p.a.)": "{:.1f}", "Sharpe ratio": "{:.2f}", "Worst month (%)": "{:.1f}", "Max drawdown (%)": "{:.0f}",
       "Average exposure": "{:.2f}", "p (Sharpe > market)": "{:.2f}"})
```

```{python}
#| include: false
S = strat.drop(index="Buy and hold")
BH = strat.loc["Buy and hold"]
vix_row = strat.loc[N["vix"]]
naive_row = strat.loc[N["naive"]]
```

Every forecaster does the same things to the portfolio: the worst month improves from `{python} f"{BH['Worst month (%)']:.1f}"`% to between `{python} f"{S['Worst month (%)'].max():.1f}"`% and `{python} f"{S['Worst month (%)'].min():.1f}"`%, and the deepest drawdown from `{python} f"{BH['Max drawdown (%)']:.0f}"`% to between `{python} f"{S['Max drawdown (%)'].max():.0f}"`% and `{python} f"{S['Max drawdown (%)'].min():.0f}"`%, while volatility ends between `{python} f"{S['Volatility (% p.a.)'].min():.1f}"`% and `{python} f"{S['Volatility (% p.a.)'].max():.1f}"`% against `{python} f"{BH['Volatility (% p.a.)']:.1f}"`% for the market. The Sharpe ratio rises from `{python} f"{BH['Sharpe ratio']:.2f}"` to `{python} f"{S['Sharpe ratio'].min():.2f}"`–`{python} f"{S['Sharpe ratio'].max():.2f}"`. But no rise is statistically significant (the smallest p-value is `{python} f"{S['p (Sharpe > market)'].min():.2f}"`), and no alpha is either (the largest t-statistic is `{python} f"{S['Alpha t-stat'].max():.1f}"`). Risk falls reliably; the extra return per unit of risk is within the noise of 26 years.

The comparison between forecasters largely reverses the accuracy ranking. The VIX alone is among the three most accurate forecasts by squared error and gives the weakest strategy (Sharpe `{python} f"{vix_row['Sharpe ratio']:.2f}"`, drawdown `{python} f"{vix_row['Max drawdown (%)']:.0f}"`%), while last month's realised variance, the least accurate forecast, gives the highest Sharpe ratio (`{python} f"{naive_row['Sharpe ratio']:.2f}"`). The exposures show how. At the end of August 2008 the VIX stood at 20.7, and because implied volatility has on average exceeded realised volatility by about three points, the VIX-only model forecast 15.9% for September; the rules built on realised volatility forecast 19–22%. The VIX rule therefore held 1.06 times the market going into September 2008, against 0.78–0.87 for the realised-volatility rules, and lost 9.1% that month against 4.4–7.2%; realised volatility in September was 51%. A forecast that is better on average can be worse at the moments that decide a strategy's outcome, and a strategy is judged on a handful of such moments.


## Robustness

```{python}
#| label: tbl-robust
#| tbl-cap: "Sharpe ratio of the managed market under alternative settings, for three forecasters. The Sharpe ratio of the market in the same sample is in the last column; p as in the previous table."
r = rob.reset_index()
r.columns = ["Forecaster", "Setting", *r.columns[2:]]
r["Setting"] = r["Setting"].replace({"baseline (cap 2, 10bp)": "Baseline (cap 2, 10 bp)"})
order = ["Baseline (cap 2, 10 bp)", "no leverage (cap 1)", "no costs", "25bp trading cost", "50bp trading cost", "excluding 2008-09 and 2020", "2000-2012", "2013-2026"]
r["o"] = r["Setting"].map({k: i for i, k in enumerate(order)})
r = r.sort_values(["Forecaster", "o"])
r["Sharpe (p)"] = r.apply(lambda x: f"{x['Sharpe ratio']:.2f} ({x['p (Sharpe > market)']:.2f})", axis=1)
r["Max drawdown (%)"] = r["Max drawdown (%)"].map("{:.0f}".format)
r["Worst month (%)"] = r["Worst month (%)"].map("{:.1f}".format)
r["Sharpe, market"] = r["Sharpe, buy and hold"].map("{:.2f}".format)
Markdown(r[["Forecaster", "Setting", "Sharpe (p)", "Sharpe, market", "Worst month (%)", "Max drawdown (%)"]].to_markdown(index=False, disable_numparse=True))
```

```{python}
#| include: false
G = rob.loc[N["garch"]]
```

The conclusion survives every variation but never becomes significant. Without leverage (cap 1) the managed market has a Sharpe ratio of `{python} f"{G.loc['no leverage (cap 1)', 'Sharpe ratio']:.2f}"` (GARCH) and a worst month of `{python} f"{G.loc['no leverage (cap 1)', 'Worst month (%)']:.1f}"`%. Trading costs matter: at 25 basis points per unit traded the GARCH strategy's Sharpe ratio is `{python} f"{G.loc['25bp trading cost', 'Sharpe ratio']:.2f}"` and at 50 basis points `{python} f"{G.loc['50bp trading cost', 'Sharpe ratio']:.2f}"`, which is below the market's `{python} f"{BH['Sharpe ratio']:.2f}"`. Splitting the sample shows that the whole Sharpe gain comes from 2000–2012 (GARCH: `{python} f"{G.loc['2000-2012', 'Sharpe ratio']:.2f}"` against `{python} f"{G.loc['2000-2012', 'Sharpe, buy and hold']:.2f}"` for the market), when volatility spikes were followed by losses; from 2013 the strategy matched the market (`{python} f"{G.loc['2013-2026', 'Sharpe ratio']:.2f}"` against `{python} f"{G.loc['2013-2026', 'Sharpe, buy and hold']:.2f}"`) and its alpha is statistically zero for all three forecasters. The strategy is a risk-reduction tool, not a source of excess return, in line with the critiques of Cederburg et al. (2020).

The volatility-managed portfolio would hold between `{python} f"{min(H['live_weight'].values()):.1f}"` and `{python} f"{max(H['live_weight'].values()):.1f}"` times the market. September has ended, but the return file used here (Kenneth French's data library) has not yet been updated, so this forecast will be scored when it is.

# Conclusion

Volatility is predictable and, for the last decade, the month-end VIX is the best single predictor; machine learning on 140 predictors does no better. Forecasts based on daily returns remain hard to beat on the loss function that matters for variance. Beyond that the data cannot separate most of the nineteen forecasters.

Better forecasts do not make better portfolios. Scaling exposure to forecast volatility reliably shrinks the worst month and the drawdown, with a worst month 10–27% smaller and the deepest drawdown 6–26% smaller, but the Sharpe ratio improves only from 0.49 to about 0.55, within sampling noise and eroded by costs, and a forecaster that is accurate on average is not necessarily the one that protects best when it counts. For an investor the sensible use is risk management: a rule of thumb that cuts exposure when recent realised volatility jumps, at modest cost, rather than an alpha strategy.

**Limitations.** Macro data are the latest vintage rather than what was known in real time. The VIX starts in 1990, so VIX-based models train on a short window early in the test. Returns of the managed portfolio assume trading the market at month-end closing prices with a fixed cost, and a borrowing spread of 0.5%, which understates the cost of leverage in stress. Strategy results rest on 26 years and two large crises, so the statistical power to detect a Sharpe improvement of 0.1 is low.
